title: Former Olympian Jeff Galloway’s legacy lives on in those he inspired to run long distances
content:
Running a 10-kilometer road race 2 1/2 years ago, Bob Moran got yanked from the course two-tenths of a mile shy of the end. He hadn’t dragged his 400-pound body to the finish fast enough.

“I said, ‘Never again,’” he recalled Friday.

Moran began following the run-walk method of training popularized by former world-class distance runner Jeff Galloway — a system that has inspired hundreds of thousands of people to run long distances by mixing walking breaks into their running. Like with so many other adherents of Galloway’s system, Moran found success.

He’s finished a 26.2-mile marathon. He’s completed a “Dopey,” a four-day series of distance races at runDisney events (5K Thursday, 10K Friday, 13.1-mile half-marathon Saturday and marathon Sunday). He has lost 115 pounds. His resting heart rate dips to 50.

He attributes the changes to one man: Galloway.

“Without a doubt,” Moran said, “he saved my life.”

Galloway, 80, died Wednesday after suffering from complications of a stroke, according to his son, Westin. Remembrances and messages of gratitude and condolences have flooded social media accounts in a volume reflecting the broad and deep impact he had.

Galloway isn’t the only proponent of fitness systems. What might have set him apart, according to Moran, was an almost unique ability to make the other participant in any encounter feel like the most important person in the world.

“It’s very hard to explain,” Moran said. “He was just a phenomenal human being.”

Erinn Hannigan was talked into doing a runDisney half-marathon with her sister-in-law in 2015, even though “when we did our running unit in high school, I got an F.” Her mother, when told of Hannigan’s half-marathon plan, said, “But Erinn, you’re not an athlete.”

When Hannigan met Galloway at her runDisney event, she told him that his training program and app made her feel like what her mother said she wasn’t.

“And he took my hand,” Hannigan recalled while trying to stifle tears, “and he held it with his other hand. And he looked me in the face, and he said, ‘Erinn, you are an athlete.’

“It took those words where someone had said, ‘You can’t do this,’ and it just erased it.”

Jack Bacheler, a teammate of Galloway’s in the 1972 Summer Olympics and on the Florida Track Club, said Galloway’s humanity was apparent even at the peak of their racing careers.

“Maybe the handwriting was on the wall back in our competitive days,” Bacheler, 82, said. “So it wasn’t a surprise that Jeff turned out to be who he was, because he was kind of like that when we were competing. … He was the kind of person who would give you the shirt off his back.”

The 1972 Olympic trials served as evidence. Galloway secured a spot on the U.S. team by finishing second in the 10,000 meters (Florida TC teammate Frank Shorter won), but Bacheler finished a non-qualifying fourth and was also disqualified for making contact with a competitor coming out of the final turn.

With the marathon trials still to come, Bacheler and Galloway devised a plan to give Bacheler a shot at a top-three finish and spot in the Munich Games. Running together, they started conservatively and worked their way into third and fourth place as they neared the finish line.

Already booked for the Olympics, Galloway didn’t challenge for third place, ensuring Bacheler got the final spot.

“That was something that I’ll be forever grateful for,” Bacheler said.

Galloway designed his run-walk system soon after the 1972 Olympics. Along with writing books, he has appeared at clinics, camps, expos and elsewhere.

“In the times I’ve interacted with him, he’d always have time to stop and talk to runners,” said Melissa Huenefeldt, a 45-year-old actuary from Olathe, Kan., currently training for her 30th marathon. “And you could tell that he was very compassionate when it came to sharing and helping runners become their best self.”

The Galloway-inspired success in distance events has cascaded to other parts of his disciples’ lives. Hannigan, a 51-year-old lawyer with a practice in Cincinnati, said the self-confidence she gained from succeeding in running fueled her decision to leave a legal practice and start one of her own — a risky move she called “crazy.”

“But I was like, ‘If I can run 48.6 miles (in a Dopey), I could do this,” she said. “‘It’s fine. I’ll figure it out.’

“Running taught me I can do really hard things.”

In a post about Galloway’s death, a Disney-affiliated Facebook account declared, “He is survived by every person who ever crossed a finish line and thought, ‘I didn’t think I could do this.’”

Followers of Galloway’s program said talking with him in person only amplified the strength they drew from reading his books and listening to him talk.

“Even if he doesn’t remember you, he treats you like you’re the most important person on the planet,” said Moran, 56, of Port Jefferson Station, N.Y. “Did he know who I was? You know what? I don’t know, honestly. But he was so positive and so reassuring that if you keep moving forward, you’ll be fine. And you know what? He was right.”

Moran wasn’t alone in saying Galloway made him feel like the most important person in the world.

“I was talking to Frank Shorter (on Thursday),” Bacheler said, “and we were talking about that very thing. And Frank said, ‘I thought I was the most important person to Jeff.’ I said, ‘Damn it, I thought I was.’”
